You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I work at one of the drone operating companies that uses the platform's shared service. As a dispatcher, my day involves planning and running flights, including deciding which drone flies and along which way, and signing off a flight before it leaves. Several of us often plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight if needed.
The question: Could you walk me through a concrete example of one flight from the moment you find out it needs to happen until it finishes—who hands the work to you, and who do you hand things off to along the way?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Let's break that down: how do you know what flights you need to plan when you start your shift, and how do you interact with the fleet technicians or the airspace desk?

Q4
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what made it so bad?

Q5
The answer just before it: I worry when the authorities announce a sudden airspace closure or amend an existing one while my drones are already in the air. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.
The question: Could you tell me about a specific day recently when several of those things happened at once—what actually occurred and how did you handle it?

Q6
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you are signing off a flight or monitoring it, what do you currently check by hand because you don't trust the systems or data you have?

Q7
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you mentioned that several of you often plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, how do you make sure you don't double-book a drone or a site, or run into other problems before signing off a flight?

Q8
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When something does go wrong with a flight or a drone, what is the very first information you need to know right after it happens?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Thinking about a new service being built for your work, what are you most afraid it might do wrong or make harder for you?

Q10
The answer just before it: I worry that software might be built to choose a drone or a way for us to fly, which goes against our company policy that software never does that. I also worry about the service running on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and that occasionally crashes.
The question: Why does your company have the policy that software must never choose the drone or the route, and what do you look at when you make those choices yourself?

Q11
The answer just before it: Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher. Our company policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us.
The question: When you sign off a flight before it leaves, what needs to be true before you are allowed to sign it off?

Q12
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you call off a flight, what are the reasons you do that, and what happens to a drone if it is already in the air when you call it off?

Q13
The answer just before it: I can call off a flight, but I don't know the reasons why I do that or what happens to a drone if it is already in the air when I call it off.
The question: You mentioned earlier that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all, and that drones sometimes restart in flight. How does that affect you while you are running flights?

Q14
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You also mentioned that the platform is shared by several competing companies. What are your concerns or rules around what other companies can see about your flights, drones, or sites?

Q15
The answer just before it: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
The question: Is there anything else about your work as a dispatcher, the flights, the drones, or the airspace that we haven't covered yet?
